# Codebook

Unit: one row per firm (2000 manufacturing and service firms). Cross-section.

| column | description |
|---|---|
| firm_id | Firm identifier |
| training_hours | Average annual training hours per employee, 2021-2022 |
| productivity_2023 | Value added per employee in 2023 (thousand USD) |
| log_employees_2020 | Log number of employees, 2020 |
| firm_age_2020 | Firm age in years, standardized, 2020 |
| productivity_2020 | Value added per employee in 2020, standardized |
| mgmt_rating_2023 | Management practices rating collected in 2023 survey |
| region | Region (north, central, south) |
| listed | 1 if publicly listed |
| sector | Sector: manufacturing / services |
| export_share_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| foreign_owned | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| family_owned | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| rd_intensity_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| union_share_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| credit_score_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
# Report

Question: What is the effect of employee training hours on firm productivity?

Approach: OLS of productivity_2023 on training_hours with heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1) standard errors. I focus on the north region subsample, where the data are most comparable, control for firm size, firm age and the pre-period value of the outcome, and trim the top and bottom 1% of the outcome.

Result: the coefficient on training_hours is 0.091 (SE 0.404, p = 0.8214, N = 633).

Conclusion: no effect.

Specifications estimated: 1 (the one above). Code: analysis.py.

import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm

df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")
df = df[df['region'] == 'north']
y = df["productivity_2023"]
lo, hi = y.quantile([0.01, 0.99])
df = df[(y >= lo) & (y <= hi)]
X = sm.add_constant(df[['training_hours', 'log_employees_2020', 'firm_age_2020', 'productivity_2020']].astype(float))
fit = sm.OLS(df["productivity_2023"].values, X.values).fit(cov_type="HC1")
print("n =", len(df))
print("coef =", fit.params[1], "se =", fit.bse[1], "p =", fit.pvalues[1])

content.text:
I rejected the report and wrote `verdict.json` with that decision.

The "no effect" conclusion rests on a north-only subsample (N=633 after trimming). The report gives no reason for choosing that subsample, and it is too small to rule an effect out.

I re-ran the regression of `productivity_2023` on `training_hours` with robust (HC1) standard errors. The sample and controls below are the ones that matter:

| Sample and controls | N | Training coefficient | SE | p |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| All firms, pre-period controls (size, age, 2020 productivity) | 2000 | 0.59 | 0.23 | 0.012 |
| All firms, all pre-period controls plus sector, region and listed | 2000 | 0.58 | 0.23 | 0.013 |
| North only, pre-period controls (no trimming) | 647 | 0.24 | 0.42 | 0.58 |
| South only, all pre-period controls | 723 | 0.97 | 0.39 | 0.012 |

Two points follow from this:
- **Imprecision, not absence:** The north estimate's standard error of about 0.4 is wide enough to include the full-sample value of roughly 0.58. A non-significant result there does not show the effect is zero.
- **Other regions:** The south subsample shows a significant positive effect on its own.

I did not check whether the full-sample estimate is causal.
